title: Benchmarks Are Memes: How What We Measure Shapes AI—and Us - Alex Duffy, Every.to
talk_summary: Alex Duffy argues benchmarks are memes that shape what model providers optimize for, and that static saturated benchmarks (MMLU, SWE-bench-style tests) miss real-world behavior. He demos a custom 'AI Diplomacy' eval where models negotiate against each other, revealing behavioral traits (scheming, naive optimism, cheap-model competence) that standard tests don't surface.

takeaways.technique: Custom behavioral eval from real work, not public benchmarks
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of trusting saturated public benchmarks, they build a bespoke scenario (multi-agent Diplomacy) that mimics the real interaction they care about and run many models through it to observe behavior.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we need more squishy like non-static benchmarks for hopefully things that matter to you

takeaways.technique: Cheap-model competence check via task-specific eval
takeaways.what_they_do: Ran 18 models through the same scenario and found a cheap model (Gemini 25 Flash) performed very well and a much cheaper model (DeepSeek R1) nearly won, despite large price gaps.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Gemini 25 Flash, man, I wish I could run every game with Gemini 25 Flash. It was so cheap and so good
takeaways.numbers: DeepSeek R1 ~200x cheaper than o3 and almost won

takeaways.technique: Behavioral profiling of models per role
takeaways.what_they_do: Observed distinct behavioral profiles: some models were naive/optimistic, others schemed or exploited weaker models; behavior differed from raw capability.
takeaways.evidence_quote: cloud models were kind of naively op optimistic. They actually none of them ever won

takeaways.what_they_do: Argues benchmarks should get harder as models improve and avoid 96-vs-98% saturation; design tasks that deepen rather than cap out.
takeaways.evidence_quote: ideally we have these benchmarks that get harder and the challenge gets deeper as the models improve

takeaways.technique: Multi-agent adversarial scenario as stress test
takeaways.what_they_do: Pitted models against each other in a negotiation game to surface coordination, deception, and exploitation behaviors invisible in single-turn tests.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there was a lot that we learned from this that that I don't think that you really learn from by having them try and solve a test
